overview: Komi names living Indigenous peoples, languages, and regional histories, not a centralized state that existed only from 1530 to 1600. Komi-Zyrian and Komi-Permyak are related but distinct identities and literary languages; the umbrella name must not erase either, and Izhma Komi claims show that Indigenous self-identification does not always match Russia’s narrow legal category. Sixteenth-century records describe communities in the Vychegda, Vym, Sysola, Udora, and Pechora regions within Muscovy. They document households, fields, hay, fisheries, woodland work, churches, taxation, petitions, travel duties, and local administration, but mostly through government and property concerns. The atlas instead draws one polygon far east, around 64 to 74 degrees east in western Siberia. It contains none of seventeen tested Komi heartland and Komi-Permyak places, including Syktyvkar, Ust-Vym, Izhma, Kudymkar, and Cherdyn. Its 1530 appearance and 1600 disappearance are dataset seams, not origins or extinction. Later ethnography helps explain living knowledge only when its dates stay visible. This card therefore combines exact map criticism, dated regional documents, explicit gaps, and continuity.

periods.title: 1530 to 1537: a misplaced polygon begins
periods.summary: The exact id first appears in the 1530 atlas as one western Siberian polygon, while tested Komi heartland places remain under other labels. No reviewed source identifies 1530 as a Komi state’s foundation. A 1537 testament belongs to documented regional life, not the artwork.

periods.title: 1537 to 1545: property records and a charter
periods.summary: The 1545 Ust-Tsilma charter granted settlement privileges and defined obligations in the Pechora region. It documents Muscovite administration at this interval boundary and offers a valuable legal window. It does not turn many Komi communities elsewhere into one bounded sovereign polity.

periods.title: 1545 to 1556: landholding and negotiated dues
periods.summary: Charters and private acts preserve claims to clearings, meadows, and other resources while authorities assessed payments and service. Their legal language reveals negotiation and inequality. It does not catalogue every household or let historians equate tax jurisdiction with a single ethnic border.

periods.title: 1556 to 1564: families appear in legal traces
periods.summary: Land and settlement records trace transfers, new clearings, and family succession. A 1564 land survey later anchors comparisons with the 1585 to 1586 cadastres. These fragments help reconstruct property and movement without supplying a complete social census or certain origin for every settler.

periods.title: 1564 to 1573: settlements change between records
periods.summary: Researchers compare the 1564 survey with 1585 to 1586 cadastres to identify newer settlements, often founded during the intervening decades. Named founders, sons, and widows help reconstruct movement, yet origins can remain uncertain and later residence does not prove ethnicity automatically.

periods.title: 1573 to 1585: lists, petitions, and local representatives
periods.summary: A 1573 to 1574 payment list and a 1582 petition illuminate taxation across Vym, Vychegda, Sysola, and Udora. Petitioners challenged assessments and named local representatives. The documents show organized communities working inside Muscovite structures, rather than an atlas-shaped Komi monarchy.

periods.title: 1585 to 1593: cadastres count households and work
periods.summary: The 1585 to 1586 cadastres enumerate villages, occupied and empty households, relatives, fields, hay, traps, fisheries, churches, and levies. They are unusually detailed fiscal records, not neutral ethnography. Their categories reveal livelihoods while leaving speech, affection, childhood, and many ordinary routines mostly unstated.

periods.title: 1593 to 1600: petitions continue as the map label ends
periods.summary: Late records include debt relief, local self-government, and obligations connected with Siberian stores and boats. In the 1600 snapshot the exact polygon vanishes beneath Muscovite mapping. That seam records a repaint, not a people’s disappearance; Komi languages and communities continue.

sections.title: Audit the misplaced atlas polygon before using it

items.text: The only exact feature is a twelve-position polygon with one ring, spanning roughly 64.0 to 73.5 degrees east and 60.1 to 66.6 degrees north. Those coordinates place the imported artwork in western Siberia, far east of the main documented Komi regions.

None of seventeen heartland controls lies inside: Syktyvkar, Ust-Vym, Yarensk, Vizinga, Ust-Kulom, Koslan, Izhma, Ust-Tsilma, Pechora, Vorkuta, Kudymkar, Cherdyn, Perm, Kirov, Veliky Ustyug, Vologda, or Arkhangelsk. Every result is false. The failed membership test is systematic, not a tiny border quibble.

Nyagan and Nadym fall inside the target polygon, while Salekhard, Berezovo, Khanty-Mansiysk, and Surgut do not. These control points describe the drawing’s western Siberian footprint in that snapshot. They do not transform residents there into Komi or prove an undocumented sixteenth-century migration.

The target shares TopoJSON arcs with Nenets, Khanty, the Khanate of Sibir, Muscovy, and the Kazan Khanate. Shared database edges reveal how layers were stitched together. They are not evidence that five governments signed matching border stones around a Komi state.

The exact id changes from absent in 1500 to present in 1530 and absent again in 1600. Twenty-one representative ownership stacks change at its appearance, and five change at its disappearance. These are snapshot seams; no reviewed source records Komi ethnogenesis in 1530 or extinction in 1600.

sections.title: Name living peoples and languages precisely

items.text: Komi can work as an umbrella name, but it must not flatten Komi-Zyrians and Komi-Permyaks into one interchangeable population. Each has its own regional history and standardized language. Their settlement regions and modern circumstances differ, so broad labels should always yield to the source’s specific group and place.

Komi-Zyrians are associated especially with the Vychegda, Sysola, Udora, Pechora, and related northern regions. Modern residence also reflects migration and administrative change. Present Komi Republic borders therefore cannot be projected backward as the edge of sixteenth-century Komi settlement or authority.

Komi-Permyaks are a related people centered farther south around the upper Kama, with Kudymkar a modern cultural center. The card discusses them when a source does, but it does not silently relabel Komi-Permyak evidence as Komi-Zyrian evidence or vice versa.

The words Zyrian and Permyak carry histories of outside classification as well as present use. Self-names, official categories, census labels, and everyday identities do not always align perfectly. A careful card names the recorded category and avoids treating one administrative checkbox as timeless cultural truth.

Medieval archaeology in the Vym and Vychegda regions identifies local cultural patterns and connections, but archaeological culture is not a passport. Pottery, settlement form, and burial practice can support regional history without proving that every excavated person used one later ethnonym.

A petition from Vym, Vychegda, Sysola, and Udora challenged how dues were assessed and involved named local representatives. It shows collective political action inside Muscovite administration. It does not establish a separate Komi crown, capital, army, or border matching the imported polygon.

The 1545 Ust-Tsilma charter and later Pechora documents show rulers granting privileges, defining obligations, and addressing settlement. Their perspective is governmental and legal. Communities negotiated within that framework, while the surviving wording tells us more about claims and dues than private conversation.

Cadastres list churches, clergy, villages, hamlets, households, fields, and taxable resources. Parish buildings were community landmarks as well as religious institutions. The records remain fiscal instruments, however, and their tidy columns should not be mistaken for a complete picture of belief or belonging.

The corpus introduction places Vym and Vychegda lands inside a centralized Russian state and explains how scribal books were compiled. That administrative fact corrects the atlas state framing. It does not erase local agency, languages, customary practice, or the uneven reach of officials.

Late sixteenth-century measures addressed local self-government and duties involving provisions and boats for Siberian ventures. Such orders linked northern communities to expanding Muscovite systems. They document imposed service and negotiation, not a voluntary merger of an atlas-shaped Komi kingdom in 1600.

sections.title: Follow rivers, fields, forests, and fisheries

items.text: Cadastres measured ploughed fields and hay meadows household by household. Grain growing and livestock care therefore belonged to the recorded mixed economy. Yields, weather, labor sharing, and hunger varied; an assessed acreage is evidence of obligation and land use, not a guaranteed full pantry.

Records count animal traps, bird nets, fishing places, and fur or fish dues alongside fields. Forest and river work complemented farming and woodland skill rather than fitting a simple farmer-versus-hunter choice. Taxable categories still omit many gathered foods, techniques, and informal exchanges.

Sysola fishing rivers and lakes could be recorded for the whole local community, showing collective access within a documented administrative setting. That entry is stronger than guessing private ownership. It cannot establish one uniform property rule for every Komi-speaking settlement or century.

Settlement archaeology preserves pottery, tools, and animal remains that help reconstruct cooking, craft, hunting, fishing, and livestock use. Preservation is selective: clay and bone often outlast bark, fibre, food, and spoken knowledge. The rubbish heap is informative, but it never filed a complete report.

Later Komi-Zyrian ethnography records herbs, berries, mushrooms, gathering, preservation, and seasonal food knowledge. It broadens the sparse fiscal archive, but its date must stay attached. A twentieth-century berry practice is a comparison, not automatic proof of the exact 1530 recipe.

sections.title: Build, make, wear, travel, and exchange

items.text: Later housing research documents log houses, furnishings, cradles, storage vessels, and regional variations among Komi-Zyrians. These objects and records help readers imagine skilled domestic work. Most date centuries after the map interval, so they cannot furnish a sixteenth-century house room by room.

Museum collections include boats, sledges, skis, hunting gear, agricultural implements, and carrying equipment. They show technical adaptation to rivers, snow, forest, and work. Object dates and collecting histories matter; the collection is not one frozen toolkit issued to every Komi family.

Wool, linen, leather, fur, dyes, and metal appear in later clothing and textile collections. Makers selected materials for particular tasks, climates, and regional styles. Some skills may be older, but a later museum label cannot independently date every seam or woven design to 1530.

Medieval Vym-region finds and settlement patterns show contacts beyond a single river valley. Imported objects and stylistic links can trace exchange, but they do not reveal every traveler’s language or motive. Trade routes were relationships and journeys, not bright lines drawn across empty forest.

Sixteenth-century documents mention boats and transport obligations because rivers connected settlements and state projects. Water travel carried people, goods, messages, and dues. The archive records demanded service better than ordinary trips, so it cannot provide a complete seasonal timetable of local mobility.

sections.title: Recover households, women, and social life carefully

items.text: Scribal books name household heads, sons, brothers, stepsons, widows, and other residents. Those relations expose multigenerational households and family succession, but a fiscal list is not a family album. Affection, conflict, fostering, marriage practice, and unpaid care usually remain outside its columns.

A 1558 to 1559 hay-meadow act names two women called Avdotia and a woman called Anna among Martynov’s children and sellers. This securely places women inside documented property transfer. One act cannot define every woman’s rights across all Komi regions.

The cadastres record widows maintaining households, sometimes with children or other relatives. Their documented presence corrects an all-male picture of settlement. Yet officials categorized homes for taxation, so women’s work in farming, food, textiles, care, exchange, and ritual remains underdescribed.

Newer settlements sometimes preserve a founder’s name and then list sons or a widow with a minor son. Researchers use those details to estimate settlement age and migration. The reconstruction is probabilistic; a named founder is evidence, not the first human ever to know that place.

Later household collections show specialized containers, textile tools, clothing, and children’s objects. They reveal labor, care, skill, and taste that fiscal documents barely mention. Because collecting often favored visually distinctive objects, absence from a museum case does not equal absence from daily life.

sections.title: Watch children learn and written language develop

items.text: A study of Komi child-rearing explicitly covers the late nineteenth to early twentieth centuries. It describes family socialization, learning work, folklore, and age-related teaching. Those themes offer comparison, but they cannot be copied backward as a complete sixteenth-century lesson plan.

Later ethnography records children’s toys and small versions of tools, suggesting learning through play and participation. Museum context supplies object evidence, not every child’s experience. A miniature implement may be educational, entertaining, or both; it does not come with a surviving report card.

Modern Komi educational materials combine authentic photographs, folklore, regional knowledge, and language for preschool teachers and families. They demonstrate active cultural transmission today. Their classroom structure belongs to the present, while the commitment to teaching children shows continuity through adaptation rather than frozen custom.

A securely dated 1510 Old Permic inscription writes the abbreviation “𐍜𐍸𐍔,” expanded by the scholarly proposal as “𐍜𐍔𐍗𐍩𐍡𐍔,” transliterated mezöse and translated “lord.” It predates the atlas interval by twenty years and is a written witness, not a quotation from every Komi community.

Old Permic was devised in the fourteenth century, written left to right, and used for Komi language materials before Cyrillic traditions prevailed. Surviving inscriptions, glosses, and religious texts are precious but uneven. Literacy did not require every household to leave a manuscript.

sections.title: Discuss healing, medicine, and health without time travel

items.text: Komi medical-folklore archives preserve healing narratives and practices recorded mainly in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. They show local interpretation, memory, and adaptation. They do not provide a securely dated prescription book for 1530, so the card refuses to invent exact period remedies.

Recorded healing knowledge can involve plants, words, household actions, specialists, and religious meanings. Researchers must carefully distinguish what narrators remembered from what earlier people demonstrably practiced. A compelling story is cultural evidence; it is not automatically a sixteenth-century clinical trial.

A 1991 indexed study concerns folk hygiene specifically among Komi-Permyaks. It can illuminate that community’s later health knowledge, but it must not be relabeled Komi-Zyrian or projected four centuries backward. Group name and publication date are part of the evidence.

Research on sanitary culture in the Komi region focuses on the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when public-health institutions and medical administration were changing. It documents that later transformation. It cannot tell us directly how a sixteenth-century household treated infection or childbirth.

Sixteenth-century cadastres count people and resources for taxation, not symptoms, disability, childbirth, or caregiving. Silence in those lists is an archival gap, not proof that illness or medical knowledge was absent. Honest history keeps the blank instead of filling it with a convenient potion.

sections.title: Manage water, waste, fire, and the missing toilet

items.text: The 1585 to 1586 Sysola survey places named settlements along the river system and records church settlements that survive in local place history. River location supports transport and fishery context. Household drinking-water treatment, contamination control, and storage remain undocumented in this source.

At Sysola fortified sites, archaeological reporting notes ash and charcoal, animal bone, broken iron, birch-bark vessel remains, and pottery. Such deposits reveal use and discard, but they do not establish a standard sixteenth-century Komi waste system or toilet arrangement across settlements.

Later museum dwellings include vessels and domestic equipment that illuminate washing, storage, cooking, and cleaning. Their documented dates prevent automatic backprojection. A bucket can be excellent evidence for its own household and still decline the job of representing everyone since 1530.

Historical sanitation research becomes much fuller in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. That later evidence helps explain changing public-health expectations, not an earlier universal norm. For 1530 to 1600, the safest conclusion is that detailed toilet arrangements remain undocumented in reviewed sources.

No reviewed sixteenth-century source securely describes a standard Komi latrine, privy, chamber pot, sewer, or waste collector. People still had ordinary bodily needs; the archive simply skipped the full bathroom tour. This card states the gap rather than installing imaginary medieval plumbing.

Old Permic is a major achievement of Komi written culture. Its surviving early inscriptions and texts connect language, religion, learning, and graphic design across centuries. The 1510 sample is small enough to verify exactly, which is better than displaying a longer phrase with uncertain spelling or translation.

Communities maintained fields, fisheries, hunting grounds, transport, worship, households, and petitions across demanding northern landscapes. Their achievement lies in coordinated life and negotiation, not in supplying a missing king for the atlas. Fiscal sources reveal organization even when they overlook much knowledge.

Research on fortified sites along the Sysola combines surface traces, excavation, erosion history, and comparisons with the 1585 to 1586 cadastre. Archaeologists build interpretations from sites rather than one national origin story. This careful, revisable method makes room for difference and uncertainty.

Komi hunting stories transmit practical knowledge, moral reflection, local identity, and humor through performance. The published ethnography concerns recent communities, not direct sixteenth-century transcripts. It nevertheless demonstrates that expertise can travel in stories as well as manuals, maps, and museum labels.

Contemporary researchers and community members combine lived experience, environmental observation, scholarship, and institutional action. This living Indigenous knowledge changes as conditions change. Continuity therefore means sustained relationships and renewed practice across generations and communities, not performing one unaltered sixteenth-century routine forever.

ending.text: The 1600 seam ends only the atlas feature. It does not end Komi peoples, Komi-Zyrian or Komi-Permyak languages, local histories, or responsibilities to northern rivers and forests. Living communities continue to teach, publish, organize, and defend cultural and environmental interests. Contemporary Komi advocacy also shows why a historical card must not trap people inside old administrative labels: extractive industry, pollution, language pressure, and political representation are present concerns answered by present action. The imported polygon cannot stand in for those communities. Its western Siberian coordinates miss every tested heartland point, and its “state” category invents a unity the historical record does not support. What continues is richer than a border: related but distinct identities, written traditions, family knowledge, regional institutions, storytelling, and collective care. The achievement at the end is endurance with change, not disappearance on schedule.
